title: Majh ki Var close
hookLine: a ballad that asks everyone to live up to their own name

lines: PORK TO ONE, BEEF TO THE OTHER.
cards: To take what belongs by right to someone else is pork to the Muslim and beef to the Hindu. That's a salok in Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, in plain English, not word for word.

It names a food each of his neighbors refuses, and it doesn't ask either one to give that refusal up. It borrows the full weight of it and points it somewhere new: at the coin, the hour, the credit that was never yours.

teach.h: GIVER, KNIFE, HARD TO BE TRUE.
teach.b: Look back over the Var as this path has walked it. It opened with the Guru as giver, a cool house of ice, a lamp. It named an age like a knife, where kings turn butcher.

Yesterday it said it is hard to be called a Muslim, and asked that mercy be the mosque. Today's salok, on the same page as yesterday's, speaks to Muslim and Hindu in one breath, each in the terms of their own practice.
It goes on, in paraphrase: the Guru and the pir will stand up for you only if you don't eat what is carrion. Talk alone carries no one to paradise; release comes from practicing truth.
Adding spice to forbidden food doesn't make it lawful. Three things to notice.
First, one measure for both. Neither neighbor is ranked above the other; each is held to a line they already keep, in a new place.

teach.h: NOT A SHRINE: WHAT YOU TAKE.
teach.b: Second, the new place is ordinary: not a shrine or a feast day, but what you take, a share, a seat, a turn in line, the credit for someone else's work.
Third, words don't settle it. The ballad has done this from its first stanzas: holding a name, king, believer, Muslim, Hindu, up beside a life and asking whether the two match.
Some readers hear it asking the same of anyone who carries a name, Sikhs included. A name is honored when the life under it takes nothing that isn't its own.
That's today's line: live up to your name.

how: Sikhs hear Majh ki Var in kirtan and katha at the gurdwara, and teachers may linger on its saloks that hold believers of every name to the same plain honesty.

games.q: what does “majh ki var close” mean?
o: the ballad's end: one measure held up to every name
the last raga in the Guru Granth Sahib
the final battle sung in Nanak's war ballad

games.q: you're speaking to two neighbors, one Muslim and one Hindu. how does the salok in the Var name the wrong of taking what isn't yours?
o: with a new rule for both.
with a food each already refuses.
with a warning about punishment only.
games.why: another's right, it says, is pork to the one and beef to the other: their own line, pointed at what they take.

practice: Walk through the day ahead in your mind, the work, the meals, the talk, and look for one place where something not quite yours could slip into your hands: someone's turn, the credit for a shared idea, the last of something meant to be split.
Don't judge it; just see yourself, at that moment, leaving it where it belongs. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath out.

wordCard.voice: Majh ki Var close. Guru Nanak's ballad in Raga Majh, a run of stanzas and saloks that holds each name, Muslim and Hindu alike, up against a life. Today's word.

orig.note: var is a ballad of stanzas; Majh is the raga it is sung in.

carryVoice: Your line: live up to your name. The Var in Majh closes on that one measure. See you tomorrow.
